lead: Passive safety saves you without driver action: structure and restraints. The crumple zone folds so occupants lose speed over a longer distance and time. The seat belt holds them; a pretensioner removes slack and a load limiter caps chest force. The airbag is a supplement, fired by the crash sensor within milliseconds. Every new car sold in India today carries this chain, from a small hatchback upward. Buses and trucks rely mostly on the structure and on belts, without airbags.
prereq: You need: Unit 3 for accelerometers and Unit 1 for the electrical supply and the squib circuit.

sections.h3: The crash pulse and the crumple zone

blocks.text: During a crash the car does not stop instantly. The front structure folds over a designed length: the crumple zone. Car deceleration against time is the crash pulse. Its area is the speed change; its length is the time restraints get.

blocks.where: a is the average deceleration in m/s², v is the impact speed in m/s, s is the crush distance in m, and t is the stopping time in s.

blocks.text: At 50 km/h (13.9 m/s) with 0.6 m crush: a = 13.9² ÷ (2 × 0.6) = 161 m/s², about 16.4 g, where g = 9.81 m/s², and t = 13.9 ÷ 161 = 0.086 s, or 86 ms. Without crush, the same speed change over a few millimetres would take under a millisecond and give about two thousand g. Even a few centimetres of crush, as in a rigid pole hit, still gives several hundred g over a few milliseconds. That gap is the point of passive safety.

The seat belt is the primary restraint. It spreads load over the pelvis and rib cage. A pretensioner, fired by the crash signal, pulls slack out in about 10 ms. A load limiter then lets the belt pay out at a few kN, so the chest avoids the peak. Belt first, bag second.

sections.h3: Inside the airbag ECU: MEMS accelerometer and safing sensor

blocks.text: The airbag ECU (electronic control unit) sits under the centre console or the floor. Its main sensor is a MEMS accelerometer: a silicon proof mass on thin springs, whose capacitance changes as the mass moves (see Unit 3, Automotive Sensors and Actuators). The output is a voltage proportional to deceleration along the car's axis, calibrated in g.

The ECU samples this about every millisecond, filters it, compares it with a stored threshold, and often integrates it into a speed change Δv. The threshold must be crossed and held for a few milliseconds, or nothing fires.

A second, independent sensor sits in series in the firing circuit: the safing sensor. It is a mechanical switch (a ball held by a magnet that closes at a few g) or a second accelerometer. The squib, a tiny heater inside the inflator, gets current only when the accelerometer and the safing sensor agree.

items: Key on: self-test. Squib continuity is checked; an open circuit stores a fault code and lights the warning lamp.
Crash: signal sampled, filtered, compared with the threshold curve.
Threshold crossed and held, safing sensor closed: fire decision.
A current pulse of a few amperes for a couple of milliseconds is sent to the squib.
The same event unlocks the doors, switches on the hazard lamps and cuts the fuel pump.

blocks.text: A capacitor inside the ECU holds enough charge to fire the bag even if the battery cable breaks in the crash (see Unit 1, Batteries, Starting and Charging Systems).

sections.h3: Inflator, venting and the other airbags

blocks.text: The squib's pulse ignites a solid propellant, which decomposes in about 20 to 30 ms into a large volume of nitrogen-rich gas; older units used sodium azide, newer ones guanidine salts.

The bag is woven nylon, folded behind a cover with a hidden seam. Gas fills it in about 25 ms after the fire signal, so it is full around 50 ms after impact. Gas then escapes through vent holes and through the fabric, so the bag softens before the occupant arrives. The bag alone cannot stop the body; it spreads the load over a larger area and keeps the head off the steering wheel and the A-pillar, while the belt does the stopping. This is the ride-down phase.

items: Driver bag in the steering wheel; passenger bag in the dashboard.
Side thorax bags in the seat or door; curtain bags along the roof rail for the head.
Knee bags under the dashboard, so the legs do not slide forward.

blocks.text: A side impact leaves very little crush distance, so side and curtain bags fire earlier, within 5 to 10 ms. Curtains stay inflated for several seconds in case the car rolls over. Rollover sensing uses a roll-rate sensor plus lateral accelerometers.

sections.h3: Occupant detection, child seats and the deployment threshold

blocks.text: Not every bump fires the bag. Each maker stores a deployment threshold, roughly a speed change in the region of 15 to 25 km/h for a frontal impact. A parking knock must not fire it: that would be costly and could injure a small person sitting close.

The full name is supplemental restraint system, SRS, and the word supplemental is literal. A belted occupant moves late and meets a bag that is already full and venting. An unbelted occupant moves early and far, and can meet the bag while its cover and fabric are still opening at high speed. That is how the device meant to protect can injure an unbelted or out-of-position person.

Occupant detection completes the rule. A pressure bladder or a capacitive mat in the passenger seat classifies it as empty, child seat, small adult or adult. If a child seat is detected, the passenger bag is suppressed. A rear-facing child seat must never sit in front of an active passenger bag.
A belt switch in each buckle drives the reminder lamp and tells the ECU which deployment path to use.

figure.caption: Crash pulse and restraint timeline: the bag is full at 50 ms, while the car still crushes.

spec.aria: Timeline in ms: crash pulse 86 ms; ECU detects by 15 ms and decides by 25 ms; inflator fills bag by 50 ms; occupant rides down after.

examples.question: A car travelling at 50 km/h hits a barrier and its crumple zone crushes by s = 0.6 m at roughly constant deceleration. Find (a) the average deceleration in m/s² and in g, (b) the stopping time in ms, and (c) state the deadline this puts on the airbag ECU and inflator.
steps: The occupant still moves near 13.9 m/s. The bag must be full and venting before the head arrives: detect near 10 ms, fire near 25 ms, full near 50 ms, inside the 86 ms pulse.
examples.answer: Average deceleration is 161 m/s² (16.4 g) and the car stops in about 86 ms; the bag must be full by about 50 ms, well inside that window.
examples.check:
v = 50/3.6
s = 0.6
a = v**2/(2*s)
g = a/9.81
t = v/a*1000
print(round(v,2))
print(round(a,2))
print(round(g,2))
print(round(t,2))

traps: Airbag is not a belt replacement: SRS means supplemental; the belt stops over 86 ms, the bag softens the last part.
Firing needs a held threshold and safing agreement; a hammer, kerb strike or door slam will not fire.
Times are milliseconds: detect 5–15 ms, fire near 25 ms, full near 50 ms, ride down after. Writing 50 s is wrong.
Pretensioner pulls slack in; load limiter lets belt out.
Classic injuries: rear-facing child seat before an active bag; unbelted or out-of-position occupant meets an opening bag.

quiz.q: Expand SRS and explain what the first word means in practice.
quiz.a: Supplemental Restraint System. The airbag supplements the seat belt; the belt is the primary restraint and the bag only spreads load during ride down.

quiz.q: Which two sensors must agree before the squib fires?
quiz.a: The accelerometer in the ECU must cross its stored threshold and hold it, and the safing sensor in series with the firing circuit must close. Both conditions must be met.

quiz.q: Why does the bag have vent holes?
quiz.a: So gas escapes after full inflation at about 50 ms. The bag softens and the occupant rides it down over tens of milliseconds instead of bouncing off a hard balloon.

quiz.q: A car at 72 km/h stops in 0.8 m of crush. Find the average deceleration in m/s² and in g, and the stopping time in ms.
A belted and an unbelted occupant sit in the same car. Explain why the unbelted one can be hurt by the bag.
quiz.a: The unbelted body moves forward early and far, so the head reaches the bag module while the bag is still deploying. The cover and fabric open at high speed and strike the head and chest. The belted body moves late and meets a bag that is already full and venting.

quiz.q: Why do side and curtain bags fire faster than frontal bags?
quiz.a: A side impact has very little crush distance, so the occupant is reached in a shorter time. Side and curtain bags therefore fire within about 5 to 10 ms, against roughly 25 ms for a frontal bag.

quiz.q: Why does the ECU check squib continuity at key-on?
quiz.a: An open squib circuit means the bag will not fire. The self-test finds it early, stores a fault code and lights the warning lamp.

quiz.q: Why must a rear-facing child seat never be placed in front of an active passenger bag?
quiz.a: The child's head is right at the dashboard. A deploying bag strikes the head directly, and the seat is designed to take load through the back of the shell, not through the head. Occupant detection suppresses the bag when a child seat is sensed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems estimate crash severity and choose an inflation level: adaptive restraint. Pedestrian airbags and external side bags appear in some markets. Event data recorders store seconds before deployment. Restraint software follows functional safety (Unit 6). Search adaptive restraint, out-of-position detection and rollover sensing.
